summary: This experimental document describes mapping between X.400 or Internet mail and Mail-11 mail, covering the Inter Personal Messaging System. Mail-11 is the mail system used on DEC VMS systems.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator between two older mail systems so a message arrives intact.

questions: how to map x.400 addresses to mail-11
subtitle: Rules for translating addresses and message elements between DECnet Mail-11, X.400 and Internet mail.

tldr.problem: Large communities ran Mail-11 (DECnet mail) and needed to exchange mail with X.400 and Internet MIME systems, but ad hoc conversions between such mail systems give unpredictable results.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines fixed mapping rules. Mail-11 addresses travel in X.400 domain-defined attributes (DD.Dnet and DD.Mail-11), X.400 addresses are embedded in a Mail-11 foreign-protocol address, and RFC 822 addresses use a quoted form. Service elements that have no Mail-11 equivalent go into an RFC822-like header in the body.
tldr.outcome: This is an Experimental memo that obsoletes RFC 1405. It leaves body part mapping to MIXER and MIME-MHS and does not discuss security.

today: RFC 2162 is Experimental and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 1405. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: Three Mail Worlds and One Gateway
sections.content:
The memo, nicknamed MaXIM-11, describes mappings that let systems running X.400 (the ISO/IEC 10021 and CCITT message handling recommendations) interwork with systems running Mail-11, also known as DECnet mail or VMSmail. Mail-11 is a protocol from Digital Equipment Corporation for real-time text messaging between systems running DECnet Phase IV and DECnet/OSI. The rules cover both DECnet addressing schemes. Only the Inter Personal Messaging System of X.400 is covered.

The motivation is community size. Large networks such as HEPnet and SPAN still used Mail-11 and wanted to reach X.400 and MIME users. The RFC warns that using non-standard mapping techniques between Mail-11 and standard mail can produce unpredictable results.

The scope is limited. The document covers the X.400 O/R address to and from Mail-11 address mapping, and the RFC 822 to and from Mail-11 mapping. Other mappings follow MIXER (RFC 2156). Body parts are not specified, since MIME encoding can be used unchanged in Mail-11 text body parts. The document obsoletes RFC 1405.
sections.plainLanguage: Three groups of people use three different kinds of mailboxes. This memo is the guide that lets a letter from one kind of mailbox reach another without getting lost.

sections.title: Mapping Message Elements
sections.content:
Mail-11 offers a very small set of message elements, so a message relayed through it could lose almost everything. To avoid that, any X.400 or MIME element with no direct Mail-11 equivalent is converted to text and placed in an additional RFC822-like header inside the Mail-11 text body part, between the Mail-11 headers and the other body parts. RFC 822 and MIME headers not covered by the memo are included as they are.

The direct mappings are simple. Mail-11 envelope elements P1-11.From and P1-11.To map to the originator and primary recipient. The header fields To:, CC:, Date and Subj: map to the primary recipient, copy recipient, submission time and subject in X.400, and to To:, Cc:, Date: and Subject: in RFC 822.

Two details need care. First, a blind copy (BCC) is only partly supported: the gateway creates a separate message with its own envelope for the BCC recipient, adds a note telling them it was a BCC, delivers it separately, and tells the TO and CC recipients that there were BCC recipients. Second, Mail-11 mail programs send a REPLY to the Mail-11 From: element and ignore Sender: and Reply-To:, so that element must hold the correct reply address. If it is not taken from the original sender, the original From information must be preserved in a From: line of the RFC822-like header, and when converting back, that line supersedes the Mail-11 one.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system only has a few boxes on its form. Anything that does not fit goes on a sticky note inside the letter, so the next translator can copy it back.

sections.title: Mail-11 Address Structure
sections.content:
A Mail-11 address is an ASCII string. In DECnet Phase IV it has the form [route] [node::] local-part, and in DECnet/OSI it is [net:] [node-clns::] local-part. Only the local part is compulsory. The local part is a username, a nickname, or a foreign-protocol address of the form prefix, separator (% or ::), then a quoted address, such as IN%"M.P.Tracy@Dicdum.cc.edu". Such foreign-protocol addresses can carry an RFC 822 address or a textual X.400 address.

Because Phase IV networks often share the same address space, the memo extends the DECnet/OSI idea of a net name to Phase IV: a unique ASCII string for the DECnet network. A registry of net names keeps them unique, and aliases are allowed. For example OMNI is the High Energy Physics and Space Physics network, with HEPnet and SPAN as aliases. Gateways must generate only official net names, using the aliases only to accept names users are used to. A small gateway table, similar to the gate tables in MIXER, pairs each net with gateway addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A Mail-11 address is like a mailing address with an optional city and street, and a person's name at the end. The memo gives each network a unique name so two towns with the same street do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Mapping to and from X.400
sections.content:
To keep the rules simple, the memo uses a fixed set of encoding rules with two domain-defined attributes (DDAs): DD.Dnet for the DECnet network name and DD.Mail-11 for the rest of the address. A Phase IV address route::node::localpart becomes the gateway's own X.400 country, ADMD and other attributes, plus DD.Dnet=net and DD.Mail-11=route::node::localpart. For DECnet/OSI the DD.Mail-11 value is node-clns::localpart. Defaults fill in a missing node (the gateway's node for the originator, the From node for recipients) and a missing net (a locally chosen first-choice network). Special characters such as quotes are encoded with a subset of the MIXER encoding, for example (q) for a quote.

Going back, if the DD.Dnet value names a network the gateway is connected to, the mapping is simply reversed. If it names an unknown network, the whole X.400 address is wrapped as gwnode::gw%"..." and sent through the gateway.

Mapping an X.400 address into Mail-11 encodes its attributes as an X.400 text address placed in a foreign-protocol address of the form gwnode::gw%"x400-text-address". When Mail-11 relays between X.400 systems, an embedded address in a domain known to the global X.400 system is mapped straight back to the original. Otherwise, it is kept in DD.Mail-11, a case the RFC calls deprecated and a temporary solution only.
sections.plainLanguage: The Mail-11 address is packed whole into two labeled slots of the X.400 form, like putting a foreign address in a box with the town name on the lid. On the way back, the box is simply opened.

sections.title: Mapping to and from RFC 822
sections.content:
Many Mail-11 and RFC 822 gateways were built independently, so several habits exist. An RFC 822 address becomes a Mail-11 foreign-protocol address, for example prot%"rfc-822-address". This direction is straightforward and unique.

The other direction has four common styles. The memo recommends one canonical form: put the entire Mail-11 address in the left-hand side as a quoted string, as "Mail-11-address"@gateway-address. This leaves the original untouched, works for DECnet/OSI and preserves the return path. Addresses with a foreign protocol are best encoded with the DD.Mail-11 and DD.dnet qualifiers, which is also the only way to give the network name for Phase IV addresses. It also warns that the percent hack is strongly deprecated.

The memo then walks the X.400, Mail-11 and RFC 822 triangle in each direction of travel. It concludes that standard Mail-11 to RFC 822 mapping is feasible, but notes that for Phase IV it may be impossible to say which DECnet community owns an address, which could make an intelligent gateway impossible.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest way to send an old-style address through the Internet is to wrap it in quotes and mail it to the gateway, which knows how to unwrap it.

sections.title: Notifications and Probes
sections.content:
Mail-11 connects directly to the destination node, so some services like address checks and delivery confirmation are possible in principle. In practice Mail-11 user agents do not support notifications or probes. Notifications can still be delivered over Mail-11, because RFC 822 and MIME notifications are MIME multipart messages and X.400 ones can be converted to the same form by MIXER.

A gateway could generate notifications or probe results for Mail-11 because of its real-time nature, but Mail-11 might only be a middle step, which reduces their value. The RFC calls this questionable, and says that any gateway doing it should state the situation and the confidence level of the result.
sections.plainLanguage: Reply receipts can travel through the old system as ordinary letters. A gateway could add its own receipt, but it should say how sure it is.
